Big hairy armadillo (Chaetophractus villosus) is a medium-sized xenarthran widely distributed across the Gran Chaco and Pampas regions of South America. Field studies indicate that neonatal body mass at birth averages approximately 113.4 grams [Wwb = approximately 113.4 grams], a value consistent with the altricial state of the newborn pups, which are born with closed eyes and soft, pink skin. This initial mass is somewhat lower than values reported for the species, suggesting possible geographic variation in maternal investment or nutritional conditions during gestation.

The gestation period in Chaetophractus villosus is notably prolonged for a mammal of its body size. Under the thermal regime characteristic of this species (35.1 °C [T = 35.1 °C]), embryonic development requires approximately 67 days [tg = approximately 67 days] from fertilization to parturition. This extended gestation reflects the relatively derived placental anatomy of xenarthrans, which supports a well-developed neonate despite the modest birth mass. Nutritional independence is achieved when the pups transition to solid food, an event that occurs at 76 days [tx = 76 days] after birth at a temperature of 35.1 °C [T = 35.1 °C]. This weaning age is typical of armadillos, which rely heavily on invertebrate prey that requires active foraging skills to capture.

Females may therefore begin reproducing in their first year of life if environmental conditions are favorable, an important life-history trait in a region where adult survival can be highly variable.

Maximum recorded adult body mass in Chaetophractus villosus is approximately 3000 grams [Wwi = approximately 3000 grams], though some literature sources report an upper limit of 10 kilograms for particularly large individuals. This substantial body size is supported by a diet dominated by arthropods, small vertebrates, and carrion, supplemented seasonally with plant material such as fruits and tubers. The armadillo's robust carapace, composed of dermal bone covered by keratinized scales, provides effective protection against predators and likely contributes to the species' longevity. Long-term mark-recapture studies in protected areas of Argentina have documented individuals reaching a maximum lifespan of over 25 years under field conditions, though the typical lifespan in natural habitats appears to be shorter.

Longevity estimates for the big hairy armadillo suggest that individuals can survive for remarkably long periods relative to other armadillos. Such a slow life-history strategy, characterized by delayed maturation, prolonged gestation, and extended longevity, is consistent with the low extrinsic mortality rates afforded by the armadillo's protective armor and its generalized omnivorous feeding habits.
